title: FRI Peer Mentor Mindsets Guide
text:
Prologue
Welcome First-year Research Immersion (FRI) Peer Mentors! Thanks for serving the next cohort of students as a mentor during the FRI Semester 1 (Research Methods: HARP 170) course at Binghamton University.
As a peer mentor, you will discover your purpose, adopt a unique mentoring style to support mentees, and develop leadership skills to support your research team. Great mentoring starts with self-awareness: knowing your own mindsets, styles, and preferences so you can adapt to your mentee and team. Each week follows a simple three-step rhythm: a brief mindset lecture or activity, a self-assessment score and reflection, and a journal entry that turns the reflection into a concrete commitment.

title: FRI Peer Mentor Mindsets Guide
text:
A Guide for You
This guide is your companion throughout the semester. Each week, you will learn about a new mindset related to peer mentoring, review your score on that mindset, and discuss how to answer the big question of the week. Each chapter has the distribution for that week’s measure and a password lookup table where you can find your own score(s).

How to find your scores
At the end of the anonymous survey you created a password. Each chapter contains a table where you look up your password to find your composite scores for that week’s measure.






NoteSave your password



Your password is the key to your individual scores all semester. Keep it in your phone notes. To change it, contact the course instructor.




How to interpret your scores
Each measure produces a composite score, the average of your responses to a set of related items (after adjusting any reverse-coded items so all point the same way).

Find your score in the password lookup table.
Locate it on the class distribution. The dashed lines mark the 33rd and 67th percentiles, and the shaded bands show the Low / Mid / High thirds of the class.
Compare where you fall relative to your peers.
Reflect using the two prompts at the end of each chapter.







NoteThere are no right or wrong scores



These measures capture orientations and styles, not ability. The purpose is self-awareness.








ImportantAbout the data



Every score, table, and figure in this draft is simulated for layout and review. Real results will replace them once the pre/post Qualtrics survey is collected.


The first numbered chapter, 1. Mentoring Style, begins the weekly measures.

title: 2. Motivational Style
text:
Your Motivational Style
Each dot is one peer mentor. These two plots split your motivation into how strongly you hold a focus and what you aim it at.
The horizontal axis is how strongly you hold that focus overall. The dashed line is the class median, so “high” and “low” mean relative to your classmates, not relative to the 1–9 scale. The vertical axis is a difference score: how much more you aim that focus at academic goals (your team’s research project) than at social goals (belonging and connection). Here the solid line at zero is a real anchor, not a class comparison. Above it you lean academic, below it you lean social, and on it you weight the two equally. Find your Promotion aim and Prevention aim in the table above.
























NoteYour style is a snapshot, not a label



The median split on the horizontal axis means roughly half the class sits on each side by construction. If you sit close to either line, small changes in a few answers would move you. The two plots are also independent: a strong promotion focus does not imply a weak prevention focus, and you can aim them at different goals. Read your position as a description of your current balance, not a fixed type.

title: 9. Conflict Mediator
text:
When each style fits
Big Question: What is your conflict resolution style?
Constructs: Conflict is simply the condition where two people’s concerns appear incompatible. It is not the same as fighting, and it is not automatically destructive. Two dimensions describe how you handle it: assertiveness (how far you try to satisfy your own concerns) and cooperativeness (how far you try to satisfy the other person’s). Crossing them gives five styles. No style is wrong. Each one works well in some situations and costs you in others.
Polarity: Win/Avoid ↔︎ Understand/Resolve, across five styles.
Measure: Dutch Test for Conflict Handling (DUTCH; De Dreu, Evers, Beersma, Kluwer & Nauta, 2001), short form. Fifteen items, three per style, rated 1 = Not at all to 5 = Very much. Each style is scored as the mean of its three items, so you get a profile across all five rather than a single label.
Every mode has benefits and costs. The skill is knowing when to use each one, not defaulting to a favorite.

title: 9. Conflict Mediator
text:
Style
Works well when
Costs you when




Competing
The issue is critical, you are clearly right, or a fast decision is needed
Overused: strained relationships, worse decisions, less buy-in from your team


Collaborating
The stakes are high enough to justify the time and both sets of concerns matter
The issue is trivial, or there is no time


Compromising
You need a workable answer quickly and both sides can give a little
It becomes the reflex, and nobody’s real concern gets met


Avoiding
The issue is minor, tempers are hot, or you need time to gather information
The problem festers and your mentees read the silence as indifference


Accommodating
You are wrong, the issue matters far more to them, or preserving the relationship is the priority
Your own concerns disappear and your credibility erodes









NoteOn the measure



The five styles come from the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument (TKI) framework. The TKI itself is commercially licensed, so this guide uses the DUTCH, a published and validated instrument covering the same five styles, drawn from concern-for-self and concern-for-others. Items are verbatim; the short form uses three of the four to five items per style, so reliability should be re-checked on this sample before results are reported anywhere beyond this guide.








TipIn Class



Role play practice.

title: 12. People Orientation
text:
Your Scores
Big Question: What is your view of people?
Constructs: An implicit theory is your working assumption about whether people can change. It matters for mentoring because it shapes how you read a struggling mentee.
Polarity: Fixed ↔︎ Growth.
Measure: ‘Kind of Person’ Implicit Theory Scale (Dweck, 1999). Eight items rated 1–6. Fixed-mindset items are reverse-scored, so a higher composite means a stronger growth mindset.

title: 13. Self-Awareness
text:
Reflect
Big Question: What is your self-awareness type?
Constructs: Dr. Tasha Eurich conceptualized this self-awareness model and its four types, based on a large-scale research program reported in Insight (2017) and in the Harvard Business Review (Eurich, 2018). Her team found that self-awareness splits into two dimensions that are largely unrelated to each other: being high on one says almost nothing about the other. Most people believe they are self-aware; Eurich estimates only 10 to 15% actually meet the criteria.
Polarity: Internal ↔︎ External self-awareness.
Measure: Self-Reflection & Insight Scale · Insight (Grant, Franklin & Langford, 2002) for the internal dimension; MCA · Fostering Independence (Fleming et al., 2013). Eurich’s model is a framework, not a published self-report scale, so the external dimension still needs a sourced instrument.
Typology. Crossing the two dimensions gives Eurich’s four self-awareness types. As in Week 1, the useful move is not picking a side but raising both:

title: 14. Paradoxical
text:
Reflect
Big Question: What is your thinking style?
Constructs: Paradox is the meta-mindset of this guide. Every earlier week gave you a polarity, and the mentor move was never to pick a side but to hold both at once: support and structure, promotion and prevention, task and relationship.
Polarity: Either/or ↔︎ Both/and.
Measure: Paradox Mindset Scale, 9 items (Miron-Spektor et al., 2018).
